analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage, strengthens equal-pay enforcement, and expands health coverage for low-income parents.
analysis.headline: The Senate Democratic leader's economic security bill, backed by 21 Senate Democrats, never left the Senate Finance Committee, and the federal minimum wage did not rise during that two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This was an omnibus bill combining several proposals: raising the minimum wage in steps to $6.65 an hour by 2003 and extending it to the Northern Mariana Islands; adding new penalties and class-action rights to equal-pay law; letting states cover low-income parents under Medicaid and CHIP with new federal money; expanding the Earned Income Tax Credit for families with two or more children; and restoring food stamps for legal immigrants. It was introduced by Senator Tom Daschle on January 22, 2001 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly seven million low-wage workers would have gotten phased raises to $6.65 by 2003. Working women could sue for back pay with compensatory and punitive damages and bring class actions, and could not be fired for discussing wages. Low-income parents of insured children could gain health coverage through Medicaid and CHIP with $2-10 billion a year in new federal funding. Working families with two or more children would get a larger Earned Income Tax Credit, and legal immigrants would regain food stamp eligibility.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $5.75 within 30 days, then $6.25 in 2002 and $6.65 in 2003, and applies the federal minimum to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands with a gradual phase-up from $3.55.

Amends the Equal Pay Act so employers bear the burden of justifying sex-based pay differences, adds compensatory and punitive damages, allows class actions, and makes it illegal to retaliate against workers who ask about or discuss wages.

Creates the FamilyCare program, letting states cover low-income parents under Medicaid and CHIP, with additional federal allotments of $2 billion in 2002 and 2003, $3 billion in 2004 and 2005, and rising to $10 billion by 2010.
Expands the Earned Income Tax Credit for eligible individuals with two or more children and simplifies its definitions.
Restores food stamp eligibility for legal immigrants and their families, reversing a 1996 restriction.
Funds $100 million a year in demonstration grants for worker technical-skills training through public-private partnerships, with employer matching funds.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum wage would bear the phased-in wage increase. Employers facing equal-pay claims would face higher damages, class actions, and new EEOC pay-data reporting. The FamilyCare expansion, training grants, and homeless-outreach grants would be paid with new federal appropriations.

drawbacks.text: The minimum wage increase raises labor costs for small businesses and low-margin employers like restaurants and retail, who would have had to absorb the phased increases to $6.65 or raise prices.

The Paycheck Fairness title adds compensatory and punitive damages and broad class-action rights to Equal Pay Act cases, which business groups argued would expose employers to costly litigation over job-category pay comparisons.
The FamilyCare title commits federal spending that grows from $2 billion in 2002 to $10 billion a year by 2011, a significant new entitlement outlay paid from the Treasury.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to low-wage workers, uninsured parents, and immigrant families are direct and large; the costs fall on a different group — employers paying low wages and the federal treasury. The main design question is whether the minimum wage increase was phased slowly enough for small employers (it rose only 50 cents a year) and whether the FamilyCare expansion's open-ended federal commitment was affordable. On balance, this was a substantial pro-worker package whose costs fall mostly on businesses and federal taxpayers rather than on the people it helps.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Finance Committee never scheduled any action on it, and it sat there until that Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Daschle introduced the bill on January 22, 2001, bundled with a Fair Minimum Wage Act, a Paycheck Fairness Act, a FamilyCare health coverage expansion, EITC changes, and food stamp restoration for legal immigrants.
21 Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans are listed as cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day it was introduced.
That was the final action: the committee never reported the bill, and no floor vote ever occurred in either chamber during the 107th Congress.
The federal minimum wage, which stood at $5.15 when the bill was introduced, did not increase at any point during that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the minimum wage kept paying $5.15 for another Congress, and opponents of expanded public health coverage avoided the FamilyCare commitment. Low-wage workers, uninsured parents, and legal immigrants received none of the bill's benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the omnibus bill on January 22, 2001 as the Senate Democratic leadership's economic security package.

for.name: 21 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Kennedy, Dodd, Clinton, Kerry, Boxer, and Durbin.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Republicans in early 2001
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 22, 2001 and took no further action — no markup, no report, no vote — for the remaining two years of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were Senate Democrats; the 49 Republicans showed no support, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill phases the federal minimum wage to $6.65 by 2003, raising payroll costs for businesses built on minimum-wage labor. The same employers kept paying $5.15 because the bill never got a vote.

The bill extends the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth for the first time, phasing up from $3.55, ending a lower local wage floor that had benefited its garment manufacturers. Workers there would have seen phased-in raises.

FamilyCare directs $2-10 billion a year in new federal funding toward covering low-income parents, revenue that flows to plans serving Medicaid and CHIP enrollees, and the bill adds a state grant program for private-market innovations like purchasing pools and reinsurance. Expanded public coverage also entrenches private plans as the delivery channel.

The bill adds compensatory and punitive damages, class actions, and EEOC collection of employer pay data broken down by sex, race, and national origin, increasing litigation and compliance costs. Workers gained a stronger remedy for unequal pay.
